name: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
role: Self-build hyperscaler and third-party capacity customer
strategy: Large cloud and AI campuses supported by regional transmission analysis, local utility arrangements and a water strategy tailored to climate. AWS is an end-user developer; its procurement is not equivalent to a merchant developer buying speculative land options.
scale: Project Rainier is described by Amazon as a 2.2 GW campus. This is a campus example, not a published minimum, and the source does not establish the facility-versus-IT basis.

publishedRequirements.fact: Amazon explains that its transmission specialists increasingly assess where adding load can benefit the grid, identifying Jackson, Mississippi and South Bend, Indiana as examples.
Project Rainier uses outside air for cooling for about 97–98% of the year, according to Amazon; climate changes the cooling economics.
Amazon committed $33 billion to Indiana data-center infrastructure and reports Indiana centers use no cooling water about 98% of the year.

inferredPreferences: Prioritize regions where the utility can structure a credible phased large-load and generation package, not merely sell a nearby transmission story.
An isolated 20–30 MW site needs a specific edge, cloud-region or expansion use case to compete with already planned campuses; that use case has not been validated.
Workforce and water-source arrangements should be evidenced alongside acreage because AWS describes regional infrastructure partnerships, not a generic national land requisition.
differentiators: Grid-system benefit is part of site selection, beyond an individual parcel power reservation.
Cooling choices are location-specific; compare outside-air hours and recycled-water opportunities rather than one national gallons/day threshold.
dealStructure: Direct acquisition/self-development and third-party capacity arrangements exist; no public willingness to buy Syncranicity’s unexercised option established.
acquisitionSignal: Current large Indiana/Mississippi investment announcements show demand and an existing pipeline; they do not establish an open site search.
searchBrief: Search utility-supported industrial campuses in AWS operating regions with expandable acreage, construction labor, identified transmission upgrades and credible renewable/reclaimed-water sourcing. Obtain a region-specific requirement before tying up land.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Proposed site cannot match the customer’s regional redundancy/network geography.
Inference: Power exists but only on a date materially later than the capacity deployment need.
Inference: Tiny first phase with no supported expansion or differentiated local purpose.
buyerQuestions: Which US cloud/AI regions are accepting third-party land proposals?
What first-phase and ultimate facility-MW blocks, network distances and earliest required service date apply?
Would a site-control assignment be reviewed, or only fee-simple land/turnkey capacity?

sources.title: Amazon approach to data center sustainability

name: Microsoft
role: Self-build hyperscaler and third-party capacity customer
strategy: Develops a geographically distributed cloud and AI estate. Its own site-selection disclosure emphasizes natural-hazard screening, economical energy and reliable telecommunications; new AI designs also alter the cooling-water requirement.
scale: No universal public land acreage or MW minimum established in reviewed sources. Avoid converting a large announced Microsoft campus into a minimum for every Azure region.

publishedRequirements.fact: Microsoft’s site-selection assessment screens floods, earthquakes, hurricanes and other natural hazards, alongside low-cost energy and reliable telecom infrastructure.
Microsoft says utilities map water, wastewater and pressure needs from the beginning and that Microsoft funds required infrastructure.
Its newer direct-to-chip closed-loop design avoids evaporation; existing sites use several cooling designs, so zero-water design is not universal to its estate.

inferredPreferences: The written hazard screen should be a separate veto document, rather than a low weight within a broad score.
Seek sites with a costed heat-rejection design: an air-cooled AI design can lower water dependence while increasing electrical and equipment needs.
A short nominal distance to fiber is insufficient; the site must fit an Azure region’s fault-domain separation and actual network routing, which are not publicly specified.
differentiators: Explicit natural-disaster minimization policy.
Utility-funded-by-customer infrastructure and community resource impacts matter even with ample headline power.
dealStructure: Self-build acquisitions and leases through specialist developers; the actual contracting counterparty depends on project. No public generic option-assignment buying policy found.
acquisitionSignal: Published operating/design commitments are current, but neither source solicits land or identifies an open US procurement window.
searchBrief: Find expandable industrial parcels within a validated Azure network region; pre-screen flood, seismic and storm exposure and provide a separate utility construction-cost schedule and cooling design.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Uncurable natural-hazard exposure.
Inference: Unverified region/fault-domain location.
Inference: Power capacity is adequate but price, collateral or network construction makes total service economics unattractive.
buyerQuestions: Is this region seeking owned land, a build-to-suit lease or third-party capacity?
Which fault-domain distances and fiber-path diversity tests apply?
Which cooling design and utility customer obligations must the acquisition case support?

sources.title: Understanding water use at Microsoft data centers

name: Google
role: Self-build hyperscaler and third-party development customer
strategy: Large cloud/AI buildout with a particularly relevant power-first Wilbarger County precedent: Google accepts an integrated construction-ready land, interconnection and new generation package, rather than evidence of line proximity alone.
scale: No standard minimum campus acreage/MW published in reviewed sources. Google’s 7,800 MW Texas generation/capacity contracting figure is energy portfolio capacity, NOT the size or load of Wilbarger or Hinds 110.

publishedRequirements.fact: Google announced a Wilbarger County data center under construction on February 24, 2026, using advanced air cooling and co-located AES clean power.
AES described construction-ready land and interconnection agreements, generation under 20-year PPAs, and long-term energy-management services for the Wilbarger campus.
Google’s Texas page lists developments in Pampa/Wilbarger in 2026 and Armstrong/Haskell in 2025.

inferredPreferences: Hinds 110 has a stronger regional comparator than a generic rural Texas site, but Google already has a controlled Wilbarger project; spare expansion land at that project may dominate any new proposal.
The differentiating product is a transferable land-plus-energy package with construction readiness and a usable heat-rejection design.
Avoid treating co-located clean generation as firm 24/7 deliverability or assuming Google wants another nearby site.
differentiators: Direct Wilbarger market evidence.
Air-cooled Texas design reduces dependence on consumptive cooling water.
AES example includes project development and long-term supply/management agreements.
dealStructure: Owned development with strategic energy/development partners; no evidence of willingness to acquire Bill’s option or pay a specific assignment fee.
acquisitionSignal: Active regional construction confirmed; no open Hinds-specific or general land requisition found.
searchBrief: Start with adjoining expansion opportunities or utility-backed nodes that improve Google’s already disclosed Texas/Iowa/Ohio/Oklahoma geography, with a written reason the existing campus cannot supply the same service.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Only 20–30 MW and no substantiated regional workload or expansion role.
Inference: New site loses to existing controlled-campus capacity.
Inference: Generation rights, interconnection or energy-management benefits do not transfer.
buyerQuestions: Is additional independent Wilbarger land needed, or is existing campus inventory sufficient?
Would an expansion parcel or integrated generation-backed site be considered?
Which facility load, firm service date and non-water cooling design are required?

name: Meta
role: Self-build hyperscaler
strategy: Large AI campuses with utility and generation partnerships. A published electric-cooperative RFI supplies unusually specific buyer requirements and is more useful than inferring a target from a generic data-center factor list.
scale: RFI: path to 540 MW+ reliable scalable energy by 2030, typically 500+ acres with expansion. Source does not label the 540 MW as IT load. Requirements belong to this co-op program, not necessarily every Meta project.

publishedRequirements.fact: The indexed official co-op RFI asks for 540 MW+ by 2030 and typically 500+ acres with expansion potential.
The RFI also requests ability to bring new grid-connected resources online, renewable opportunities, closed-loop cooling water, community support and construction/operations workforce.
Meta’s energy page describes funding grid upgrades and new resources, including clean-energy and nuclear agreements.

inferredPreferences: Hinds 110 alone is below this RFI’s typical land envelope; adequate 20–30 MW capacity would not cure the scale mismatch.
A co-op-backed assemblage and credible generation plan are much better search starting points than low-priced isolated acreage.
The site must preserve control over contiguous expansion land and environmental buffers, not just gross acres.
differentiators: Explicit dated energy delivery target and land scale.
Electric-cooperative program is a distinct procurement lane.
RFI appears in official search index, but direct page retrieval returned 404; current intake availability must be reconfirmed.
dealStructure: Direct campus development and utility/generation partnerships. No evidence Meta purchases small speculative purchase-option assignments.
acquisitionSignal: Specific public co-op solicitation indexed as of review; intake status not confirmed because direct access failed. This is not a response or interest in any candidate.
searchBrief: Search 500+ contiguous-acre co-op service areas with a path to 540 MW+ by 2030, expandable transmission/generation, water and workforce; smaller neighboring tracts only as demonstrable campus expansions.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Standalone 110 acres / 20–30 MW offering pitched as satisfying this RFI.
Inference: No cooperative or other credible utility-led delivery plan.
Inference: Assemblage cannot be controlled on one realistic schedule.
buyerQuestions: Is the co-op RFI currently accepting responses?
Does a staged 540 MW plan qualify and what is the first energization block?
Can the land be optioned/assembled by a third party and what transfer/reliance rights are required?

sources.title: Meta electric-cooperative site RFI (indexed; direct retrieval 404)

name: Apple
role: Self-build owner-operator; selective footprint expansion
strategy: Owns and develops a relatively selective data-center estate supporting Apple services. Environmental reporting gives strong design/energy preferences but no open national land-acquisition mandate.
scale: Apple’s 2026 report identifies eight Apple-owned data centers following Waukee’s October 2024 opening. No public universal acreage, first-phase MW or rack-density acquisition threshold found.

publishedRequirements.fact: Waukee opened October 2024; Apple reports 100% renewable electricity since opening and works with MidAmerican Energy wind sourcing.
Apple’s 2025 report describes water-treatment, server and cooling-control upgrades across Maiden, Prineville, Reno and Mesa.
Apple reports Alliance for Water Stewardship certification across most owned data centers; its 2025 report distinguished seven certified sites from its newly opened eighth.

inferredPreferences: An appropriate pitch needs an identified Apple capacity/location need; cheap power alone cannot explain a new isolated site.
Energy contracting and watershed stewardship should be modeled at site level; state renewable percentages are insufficient.
Neighboring expansion opportunities around known campuses may be more credible than a first-entry rural market, but no current expansion mandate is confirmed.
differentiators: Small, selective self-owned footprint rather than national merchant-colocation leasing.
Wind sourcing and site-level water stewardship are directly evidenced.
dealStructure: Owned campuses; no public acceptance criteria for land options, assignment fees or unsolicited broker submissions found.
acquisitionSignal: Waukee is a recent completed expansion, not an available site or evidence of an imminent new acquisition.
searchBrief: Search only after Apple validates a location/capacity gap; prioritize campus-adjacent expansion or established Apple regions with tractable renewable contracting and documented watershed impacts.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: No specific capacity need in the proposed region.
Inference: A site’s renewable claim is unsupported by a procurement path.
Inference: Water constraints cannot be cured with a design Apple is prepared to use.
buyerQuestions: Is Apple seeking additional owned US land in this region?
Does the mandate favor campus adjacency, redundancy separation or a new region?
What energy procurement and water stewardship evidence is needed for first review?

name: xAI / SpaceXSI Memphis
parentGroup: Official x.ai Memphis pages currently use SpaceXSI; legal transaction parent must be verified
role: AI self-builder / infrastructure customer
strategy: Rapid large-scale AI cluster deployment anchored in the Memphis region, with substantial on-site energy infrastructure. Current official pages use SpaceXSI branding; do not count xAI and that name as independent buyers.
scale: Official July 2026 update describes a 1.2 GW permanent power plant for Southaven. That is generation nameplate, not proven net IT capacity or a general acquisition minimum.

publishedRequirements.fact: The Memphis page describes Colossus and a 2026 target of 1 million GPUs, alongside local utility/government coordination.
July 30, 2026 update says all 69 temporary mobile turbines must be removed by July 2027 as a permitted 1.2 GW permanent plant is built.
The update describes 41 permanent turbines and noise/emissions controls; these are project-specific developer statements, not independent permit-compliance conclusions.

inferredPreferences: Within-region expansion, grid/gas co-development and rapid industrial conversion are materially more relevant than an isolated 20 MW greenfield option.
Air permits, gas transportation, noise control and generation lead times remain decisive even if sufficient grid MW are assumed.
A fast-track schedule must include binding permit conditions; temporary generation cannot be treated as an indefinite substitute for lawful permanent supply.
differentiators: Very high-density AI cluster geography and rapid deployment.
Industrial conversion and on-site generation strategy create a different buyer specification than ordinary multi-tenant colo.
dealStructure: Self-build property and energy development; an option assignment or new-region project needs explicit procurement validation.
acquisitionSignal: Active Memphis/Southaven buildout, but no public national land solicitation and no interest in Hinds established.
searchBrief: Search Greater Memphis industrial sites with usable structures, expansion yards, proven gas and grid paths, air-permit viability and a demonstrable network connection to the existing cluster.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Geography is outside the required cluster and lacks a validated new-region mandate.
Inference: Fast deployment depends on unpermitted temporary generation.
Inference: Noise, air or gas supply prevents the required operating envelope.
buyerQuestions: What legal entity and procurement group currently acquires expansion sites?
Must proposed land connect to Colossus within a specified latency/fiber budget?
Is a powered shell, existing factory or greenfield campus desired?

name: Cologix
parentGroup: Private developer platform; parent ownership not reverified in this pass
role: Interconnection and hyperscale-edge developer/operator
strategy: Builds network-neutral interconnection hubs and larger Scalelogix capacity. For land sourcing, metro network gravity and proximity to existing customers can outweigh cheap rural land.
scale: February 2026 Ashburn acquisition: 38 acres; 85 MW initial power and more than 300 MW potential over time; preliminary planning around 2030. These are campus plans, not company-wide minimums or current delivered MW.

publishedRequirements.fact: Cologix acquired 38 acres on Beaumeade Circle in Ashburn, describing industrial zoning, dense fiber and proximity to existing digital infrastructure.
The announced program serves hyperscale, AI-ready, enterprise, carrier and locally based demand and emphasizes interconnection and hybrid-cloud architectures.

June 2026 announcement identifies new Orange Township and Johnstown campuses and more than $1.1 billion of initial-phase investment. This substantiates central Ohio geography while adding competing controlled supply.

inferredPreferences: In Ashburn the expensive connected location is itself the product; distant surplus power would not substitute for the same interconnection economics.
The 2030 planning horizon shows willingness to land-bank strategically, but should not be generalized to a founder’s short option term.
A suburban Ohio or Denver candidate needs two real fiber routes and a link to Cologix customer ecosystems.
differentiators: Small acreage can be strategic when urban fiber density is exceptional.
Planning date is far later than the initial land purchase, illustrating how buyer holding capacity differs from Syncranicity’s.
dealStructure: Direct land acquisition for owned campus development demonstrated; acceptance of option assignments not disclosed.
acquisitionSignal: February 2026 Ashburn acquisition is strong land-buying evidence but adds already controlled competing supply.
searchBrief: Search industrially entitled metro parcels near major carrier interconnection with a staged utility plan; do not use the Ashburn 85 MW as a universal intake threshold.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Low-cost land is outside the necessary network/enterprise market.
Inference: Fiber is technically nearby but diverse paths or cloud onramps cannot be constructed.
Inference: Option term expires years before the buyer’s land-bank development decision.
buyerQuestions: Which Scalelogix/interconnection markets have an unmet land requirement?
What dark-fiber routes, round-trip latency and carrier access must a new parcel support?
Is strategic land banking or near-term ready-for-service the current priority?

sources.title: Cologix Orange Township and Johnstown expansion

name: H5 Data Centers
parentGroup: H5 platform; certain portfolio acquisitions joint with Novacap
role: Developer/operator; carrier-hotel and enterprise-campus acquirer
strategy: Combines new development with acquisition and densification of network-rich existing buildings. It has a tangible preference for strategically important carrier ecosystems, not merely raw capacity.
scale: Observed examples: 255,000 sq ft/42 MW Ashburn build; approximately 225,000 sq ft Albuquerque carrier hotel. MW basis unspecified in release index; neither is a minimum.

publishedRequirements.fact: H5 announced February 2026 acquisition of Buffalo, Nashville and Tampa centers from 365 through a Novacap JV, emphasizing carrier density.
Its news archive documents Ashburn new construction, San Antonio carrier-hotel expansions and Phoenix phases, as well as internet-exchange/cloud-connectivity partnerships.

inferredPreferences: A former enterprise data center with reusable electrical/cooling systems and networks may be more attractive than comparably priced agricultural acreage.
For carrier-hotel acquisitions, tenant/network stickiness matters; for new campuses, an anchor customer and expansion runway matter.
Former enterprise assets need technical audit before claiming speed-to-market: electrical topology and usable IT space may constrain a high-density conversion.
differentiators: Both greenfield and existing-building acquisition paths verified.
Carrier-hotel value depends on established ecosystem, difficult to recreate on rural land.
dealStructure: Direct building/land acquisitions, joint-venture capital and powered-shell/build-to-suit offerings; no option-assignment policy publicly established.
acquisitionSignal: 2026 portfolio purchase confirms active acquisition activity; an identified open greenfield land mandate remains unknown.
searchBrief: Find underused enterprise campuses or strategic metro carrier buildings with expansion land, tested fiber diversity and a market-specific customer case; separate a reuse thesis from a new-build thesis.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: No interconnection/customer advantage in a target metro.
Inference: Existing infrastructure cannot be reused economically.
Inference: Raw land proposal lacks an anchor use and competes against H5 owned expansion space.
buyerQuestions: Does H5 currently favor carrier-hotel acquisitions, powered shells or greenfield sites in this market?
What minimum reusable electrical/cooling condition is required?
Can a phased land/building option be assigned into an H5 JV?

name: 365 Data Centers
parentGroup: 365 platform; 2026 development partnership with Aphorio Carter
role: Operator/development partner; adaptive-reuse emphasis
strategy: A 2026 partnership with Aphorio Carter targets identifying, converting and developing AI-ready facilities; 365 would operate them long-term while its partner contributes real-estate/development capabilities.
scale: Approximately 200 MW aggregate initial pipeline, six sites; 50 to 200+ kW per cabinet; 9–24 month indicated delivery after May 2026 announcement. Pipeline MW basis not identified; not a per-site minimum.

publishedRequirements.fact: May 2026 release identifies Aurora and Simpsonville LOIs and additional planned LOIs in Trumbull, Louisville, Harrisonburg and Columbus.
Facilities are designed for liquid-to-chip cooling at 50–200+ kW/cabinet; availability is subject to final contracts/internal approvals.
Trumbull’s official August 2026 update describes renovation of an existing center with no additional grid draw, noise, water or footprint, and 365 as prospective 15-year tenant.

inferredPreferences: Existing industrial/data-center assets with usable service and rapid conversion are stronger than bare land requiring a full permitting/construction cycle.
The operator may not be the actual purchaser; qualification should involve Aphorio Carter’s acquisition team.
Do not infer that every announced 200 MW pipeline opportunity is already contracted or that stated 9–24 months remains achievable.
differentiators: Published target geographies and rack-density range.
Actual separation of landlord/developer and long-term operator.
Trumbull illustrates a constrained reuse project, not permission to increase all infrastructure.
dealStructure: Developer/owner partnership plus long-term operating/lease role; ask who can acquire/accept the control instrument.
acquisitionSignal: Named 2026 LOIs and development partnership constitute a specific growth program; available capacity and additional demand require confirmation.
searchBrief: Source powered buildings or rapid-conversion industrial sites in six named markets, documenting reusable plant, liquid-cooling retrofit costs and feasible 50–200+ kW racks.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Greenfield schedule cannot meet conversion-led deployment window.
Inference: Only nameplate power; no budget for higher-density cooling and electrical distribution.
Inference: Site already targeted under another party’s LOI.
buyerQuestions: Which of the six markets still need uncommitted sites?
Who buys the land—365 or Aphorio Carter—and what should an assignment package contain?
Is a powered shell sufficient, or must existing commissioned plant be reusable?

name: TierPoint
parentGroup: TierPoint platform; financing ownership not reverified
role: Enterprise developer/operator and campus acquirer
strategy: Enterprise colocation transitioning into larger AI deployments, with strong acquisition-and-expansion precedent. It can value existing customer ecosystems and operational infrastructure as much as vacant acreage.
scale: TekPark 137 acre campus with 100 MW power expansion; Fort Worth acquired 208,000 sq ft with 5 MW available, 8 MW near-term and 18 MW long-term plans. These are project figures; IT / facility basis not consistently specified.

publishedRequirements.fact: October 2025 announcement describes buying its formerly leased TekPark campus and funding 100 MW expansion targeted for second-half 2026.
Fort Worth 2024 acquisition offered staged 5/8/18 MW and both conventional colocation and GPU/high-density deployment use cases.

inferredPreferences: A modest first phase with a practical campus ramp can fit; a 100 MW end-state is not required for every TierPoint transaction.
Look for former enterprise facilities or land near existing TierPoint demand where reuse shortens delivery.
Expanding an occupied leased campus reduces customer-migration risk; a new rural greenfield site must overcome that advantage.
differentiators: Strong proof of acquiring a leased operating campus.
Both 5 MW entry and 100 MW campus expansion examples.
Demand-backed high-density cooling appears more important than a universal rack-density rule.
dealStructure: Fee-simple acquisitions of facilities/campuses and financed expansion. No public generic assignment-fee criteria found.
acquisitionSignal: Recent financed TekPark acquisition and Fort Worth expansion demonstrate acquisition appetite, but not interest in a specific marketed tract.
searchBrief: Prioritize existing regional enterprise facilities with expansion land, useful plant and identified large customer demand; record cost to migrate or retain tenants and deploy liquid cooling.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: No customer case beyond cheap megawatts.
Inference: Expansion requires replacing most existing infrastructure without a time advantage.
Inference: New region loses to current campus expansion.
buyerQuestions: Is there a power/space shortage in one of your existing markets?
Could an initial 5–10 MW campus with documented expansion fit?
Would you prefer acquiring an operating facility or a new build-to-suit?

name: Expedient
parentGroup: Expedient platform; owner not reverified in this pass
role: Enterprise cloud/colocation operator and facility acquirer
strategy: Expands managed cloud and regional colocation capacity through existing enterprise facilities. Its Columbus purchase demonstrates a practical smaller-campus demand profile; it does not establish a national speculative greenfield land mandate.
scale: 2024 Columbus acquisition announced 3 MW initial and 7.5 MW eventual capacity. Current facility page reports CMH3 at 7 MW critical IT, with 10 MW generators and 2N UPS; power categories and reporting dates must not be mixed.

publishedRequirements.fact: Expedient acquired the former Nationwide facility near Columbus in February 2024, adding its fifteenth US data center.
The facility supported more than 33,000 physical servers and provided staged power expansion rather than a gigawatt campus.
Current Columbus page reports CMH3 at 7 MW critical IT, 2N UPS, 10 MW total generator capacity and four on-net carriers, separate from the 2024 acquisition announcement’s staged plan.

inferredPreferences: A reusable enterprise facility with a regional customer base may offer a more compelling acquisition case than vacant industrial acreage.
Search for power/density headroom and the cost of integrating the property into a managed-cloud network, not just total acreage.
Its published acquisition is older; confirm whether capacity remains needed before building a costly site-specific package.
differentiators: Single-digit-MW initial deployment precedent.
Former corporate data-center reuse supports faster delivery but requires engineering and tenant/service diligence.
dealStructure: Direct acquisition of enterprise facilities demonstrated. No published willingness to buy raw-land options established.
acquisitionSignal: Columbus expansion is verified but is not a current open procurement notice. 2026 product releases focus on enterprise cloud/AI services rather than new land acquisition.
searchBrief: Locate former corporate data centers or powered industrial conversions in established enterprise markets with 3–10 MW expansion potential, diverse network paths and reusable MEP; these quantities are analyst search hypotheses, not buyer requirements.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Standalone rural location lacks local enterprise or disaster-recovery demand.
Inference: Existing facility requires rebuilding its entire power/cooling chain.
Inference: Proposed scale exceeds a realistic pre-leasing or cloud deployment plan.
buyerQuestions: Which regions have an unmet enterprise colocation requirement?
Is acquisition of an operating or decommissioned corporate center preferred?
What data-hall geometry, compliance and network integration would disqualify a facility?

sources.title: Expedient adds fifth Ohio data center

name: Lightedge
role: Enterprise hybrid-cloud developer/operator and acquirer
strategy: Emphasizes secure, compliant enterprise hybrid cloud and disciplined expansion where it already has customers and operating depth. The strongest current signal is buying a fully pre-leased center rather than taking speculative land risk.
scale: April 2026 acquisition: 3 MW critical IT, Tier III, fully pre-leased and turnkey. A separate Kansas City facility page advertises 20 MW critical IT capacity; these are distinct assets, not a general minimum.

publishedRequirements.fact: Lightedge acquired a 3 MW Tier III Kansas City facility that was fully pre-leased and had rights of first refusal already in place.
The same release describes growth in existing markets and demand from financial services, insurance, healthcare and logistics.
It identifies a 2024 Chaska acquisition and Connectria acquisition; Involta/Ark is a different platform and is not counted as Lightedge.
Its existing Kansas City facility page identifies 9050 NE Underground Drive and advertises 20 MW critical IT capacity; the separate 3 MW acquired facility required no capital buildout.

inferredPreferences: A pre-leased or customer-backed expansion is more credible than a raw-land proposition without revenue visibility.
Compliance and geographic proximity to regulated customers may dominate a rural power discount.
A small site can be commercially useful, but only if plant redundancy, operating standards and network connections meet the intended enterprise use.
differentiators: Explicit market-driven growth within existing roots.
Fully pre-leased acquisition with ROFR demonstrates commitment before large incremental capital.
Regulated-industry compliance is a commercial requirement, not a marketing afterthought.
dealStructure: Direct acquisition of purpose-built facilities; potential development structure must be confirmed. No public standard for buying unexercised options.
acquisitionSignal: April 2026 acquisition supplies current evidence of active investment, with a strong preference signal for contracted demand.
searchBrief: Search existing metro facilities or contiguous expansions near Kansas City, Des Moines and other confirmed markets; seek anchor tenants, reusable Tier III-class infrastructure and a costed modernization plan.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Uncontracted rural greenfield thesis offers no defensible enterprise demand.
Inference: Facility cannot satisfy target customer compliance or resilient operations.
Inference: An existing campus can supply capacity sooner and cheaper.
buyerQuestions: Would you underwrite an unleased site or require an anchor commitment?
Which markets and customer sectors have unsatisfied demand?
Would you acquire a building/land option, or prefer a commissioned facility?

name: US Signal
role: Fiber-integrated data-center operator and expansion developer
strategy: Coordinates data-center expansion with its own fiber infrastructure and regional enterprise/cloud products. Existing network reach and customer access are part of the acquisition logic, not independent checklist items.
scale: 2025 program added 3 MW commercial power in Detroit and 6 MW in Des Moines. Aurora plans distinguish 6 MW commercial power from 4 MW UPS-supported capacity, with longer-term 8–10 MW total-facility ambition.

publishedRequirements.fact: US Signal announced a $200 million program with data-center additions and more than 1,000 miles of dense fiber/conduit.
Aurora, acquired December 2025, is receiving UPS, generator and cooling upgrades, plus a new link to Oak Brook.
Aurora phase two explicitly separates utility/commercial capacity from UPS-supported capacity; future 8–10 MW is a target, not current capacity.

inferredPreferences: Parcels or buildings on an economic extension of its backbone rank above disconnected low-cost land.
A 10–20 MW first phase may already be above several cited regional upgrades; secure an actual demand brief instead of assuming more MW is always better.
Network construction, resilient IT capacity and customer migration costs should be modeled as one project.
differentiators: Useful public separation of facility and UPS-supported capacity.
Owned-network expansion is tightly coupled to data-center investments.
dealStructure: Facility acquisition followed by phased upgrades; no public blanket raw-land or option-assignment program.
acquisitionSignal: June 2026 Aurora expansion is a current capital program but consumes funds and customer demand within an already owned site.
searchBrief: Search Midwest enterprise campuses connected to US Signal routes, with room for redundant plant and a feasible path to additional critical IT load; validate demand beyond existing-campus upgrades.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Network extension erases power/land savings.
Inference: Power figure ignores UPS/cooling limits.
Inference: No incremental customer requirement after current expansion program.
buyerQuestions: Where does the current network/customer pipeline require another site?
What critical IT load and utility-feed redundancy are needed?
Would a former enterprise center with expansion land beat existing campus expansion economics?

name: Bluebird Fiber (formerly Bluebird Network)
parentGroup: Bluebird Fiber; do not conflate with similarly named Denver site-originator
role: Fiber-network operator and regional colocation facility developer
strategy: Operates regional data centers whose value is tied to Bluebird fiber, peering and resilience. Its underground Springfield location is a special-purpose asset, not evidence that ordinary farmland is interchangeable with its campuses.
scale: Published offerings include cabinet/cage/room colocation and 8,000–10,000 square feet available whitespace. No current published greenfield acreage/MW acquisition threshold established.

publishedRequirements.fact: Current data-center page identifies Springfield Underground and Quad Cities sites, with multiple utility feeds, backup systems and network services.
Published Springfield latency examples are 5–8 ms to Kansas City, 8–10 ms to St Louis and 10–12 ms to Chicago; these are service examples, not universal site-selection limits.
October 2026 release describes a multi-year optical-network upgrade supporting 100–400G services and diverse Midwest routes.

inferredPreferences: Sites should improve a known route, peering location or customer catchment; this buyer is not automatically a taker for 20–50 MW rural land.
A proposal for resilience/disaster recovery needs both geographic separation and customer-usable network latency.
The latest investment signal concerns fiber upgrades, so any new real-estate acquisition appetite needs direct confirmation.
differentiators: Regional low-latency network and disaster-resilience differentiation.
Underground limestone facility is an unusual existing-site feature, not a general construction requirement.
dealStructure: Own/operate regional centers; current public land-option acquisition or national development mandate not found.
acquisitionSignal: 2026 network investment is verified; no new campus land solicitation was located.
searchBrief: Search existing regional carrier or enterprise facilities on Bluebird routes with customer demand, redundant power and a clear resilient-network role. Treat as secondary discovery, not a first wave raw-land buyer.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: No network/customer synergy.
Inference: Rural facility cannot offer credible geographic or latency benefit.
Inference: Large speculative campus exceeds evidenced expansion strategy.
buyerQuestions: Is Bluebird actively acquiring/developing additional colocation real estate?
Which fiber nodes or customer areas need capacity?
Would a partner own the site while Bluebird supplies network and operations?

name: Ark Data Centers (formerly Involta)
role: Regional edge developer/operator
strategy: Purpose-built enterprise and hyperscale-edge facilities in regional markets. Ark rebranded from Involta in 2024 and should be counted as one platform; it is not Lightedge.
scale: 2024 Green Bay program contemplated expansion to 20 MW. Current facility page describes 10 enterprise-class Tier III data centers across seven edge markets, although its location list spans several cities. No general minimum acreage/MW published.

publishedRequirements.fact: Involta rebranded as Ark in May 2024, citing expansion for enterprise and hyperscale-edge capacity and a Green Bay campus growth plan up to 20 MW.
Ark describes purpose-built expandable centers, separate-source power feeds, carrier-neutral connectivity and geographic safe zones.

inferredPreferences: This is a better size match for a genuine 10–25 MW regional requirement than a Meta-style 500-acre search.
A lower-cost regional site still needs local enterprise demand or a validated edge customer; proximity to an existing Ark market is helpful but not sufficient.
Search for a geography/resilience/network gap the existing campus cannot fill.
differentiators: Explicit regional edge-market strategy.
Expandable, redundant enterprise facilities rather than energy-only campuses.
Tucson presence offers a local relationship/discovery avenue for Bill, but does not establish demand for Benson.
dealStructure: Development and campus expansion; no public generic option-assignment acceptance policy found.
acquisitionSignal: Published Green Bay expansion and purpose-built development capabilities, but no new parcel solicitation located in this review.
searchBrief: Search industrial parcels or reusable facilities near Ark edge markets with meaningful network diversity, resilient utility topology and a customer-backed 10–25 MW phase; scale is a hypothesis informed by Green Bay, not a mandate.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: No edge/enterprise demand within usable network geography.
Inference: Only one practical power or carrier route.
Inference: Hazard exposure conflicts with resilient regional design.
buyerQuestions: Which edge markets currently need greenfield capacity?
Would a 10–25 MW phased campus fit today’s pipeline?
What evidence distinguishes an attractive regional site from a location already served by existing facilities?

name: DāSTOR
role: Enterprise colocation operator and facility acquirer
strategy: Boutique enterprise and hybrid-colocation platform focused on the Mid-Atlantic. Its demonstrated expansion path is acquiring purpose-built facilities with connectivity and redundant plant, not nationwide speculative raw land.
scale: New Castle acquisition offers more than 30,000 square feet of raised floor. No universal MW/acreage threshold found; published 2N+1 UPS and N+1 cooling describe that facility.

publishedRequirements.fact: April 2024 purchase of 3 Boulden Circle, New Castle added a fifth facility between Ashburn and New York/New Jersey.
The acquisition release cites dense connectivity, Delaware IT equipment tax advantages, 2N+1 UPS and N+1 cooling.
Current company page positions DāSTOR as a boutique provider with direct access to its operating engineers.

inferredPreferences: An existing facility with a demonstrable Mid-Atlantic network position is more actionable than a Texas or Arizona greenfield option.
A Dover site needs a measured network/customer case; being in Delaware alone does not replicate New Castle’s I-95 location.
Acquisition underwriting should include equipment condition, customer commitments and cost to add high-density cooling.
differentiators: Specific I-95 market positioning.
Enterprise service and hands-on operations rather than hyperscale-only infrastructure.
dealStructure: Purpose-built facility acquisitions; new development/ground-lease appetite unverified.
acquisitionSignal: Historical 2024 expansion established; no current public land request found.
searchBrief: Search Mid-Atlantic enterprise data-center conversions or modest expansion tracts near existing fiber routes and customers. Require confirmation that new construction is accepted before spending on greenfield diligence.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Outside the validated Mid-Atlantic footprint.
Inference: Greenfield economics fail against reusable existing facilities.
Inference: Redundancy/connectivity cannot support regulated enterprise workloads.
buyerQuestions: Are you reviewing new construction or only existing facilities?
Which Pennsylvania/Delaware submarkets need additional capacity?
What critical IT load, redundancy and fiber economics are required?

name: Lincoln Rackhouse / Lincoln Data Center Group
role: Real-estate developer, investor and build-to-suit partner
strategy: Combines real-estate capital and development capability with land, fiber and power partners. This is a particularly relevant counterpart for a land-originator structure when the site contributes something scarce.
scale: Red Oak announced 131 entitled acres, more than 800,000 square feet, and up to 540 MW total power. The release says total power, not IT load; these are project plans, not a corporate minimum.

publishedRequirements.fact: January 2025 partnership has Gigabit Fiber contribute 131 fully entitled acres while Lincoln supplies capital, financing and development expertise.
Lincoln’s data-center practice explicitly provides acquisitions/investments, site selection, build-to-suit development, fiber procurement and power acquisition/distribution.

inferredPreferences: A land contribution or JV can be more aligned with Lincoln’s evidenced structures than assuming a simple option flip.
The valuable input is entitled, connected land with a specific capital plan; bare acreage without control or an execution role is weaker.
Dallas cluster proximity and fiber partnership were part of the Red Oak thesis. Rural Texas cannot be substituted without a new customer / network case.
differentiators: Direct precedent for land contribution plus developer financing.
Can structure across real estate and infrastructure rather than only buy a finished center.
dealStructure: Acquisition, investment, build-to-suit and JV/land contribution demonstrated. No guarantee it buys unexercised options; economic participation and liabilities require negotiation.
acquisitionSignal: 2025 Red Oak transaction is clear partnership evidence, but its land is already controlled and is not an available opportunity.
searchBrief: Search metro-adjacent entitled campuses with fiber partnership potential and a staged utility plan; prepare a land/control contribution case that explains how Lincoln’s capital unlocks a specific customer project.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: No unique site contribution beyond a marked-up listing.
Inference: Entitlements or fiber rights cannot transfer.
Inference: Founder cannot fund/control the position through partner review.
buyerQuestions: Would Lincoln evaluate an assignable option or require land ownership before a JV?
Which markets and campus scales are currently capital-approved?
What entitlement, power and fiber milestone must the land partner deliver?

name: ScaleMatrix
parentGroup: ScaleMatrix Holdings; ownership not independently reverified
role: High-density colocation/cloud operator; development through facilities and partners
strategy: Differentiates through cabinet-level dynamic-density technology and enterprise/HPC services. Its technology can operate within a partner facility; that is materially different from a mandate to buy raw land.
scale: Official homepage advertises dynamic 1–52 kW per cabinet. This is a product specification on a page with older content, not a verified 2026 ceiling or a land-buying minimum.

publishedRequirements.fact: ScaleMatrix advertises dynamic cabinet densities from 1 to 52 kW and high-performance cloud/colocation services.
A historical Seattle launch used a partnership with wholesale provider Centeris, illustrating a partner-campus expansion route.

inferredPreferences: A powered shell or partner facility with a local HPC/customer case is likely more relevant than a large independent rural campus.
Confirm current density/cooling requirements directly before using the older public specification to design a new AI site.
The need may be leasing/deploying capacity rather than buying land; ask this before any parcel diligence.
differentiators: Dynamic density at the cabinet level.
Partner-hosted deployment can separate the land buyer from the service operator.
Public expansion evidence is dated; current acquisition appetite remains unverified.
dealStructure: Facility/partner deployments; no recent public raw-land acquisition mandate established.
acquisitionSignal: Operating product capability verified, but cited expansion precedent is historical and should not be treated as fresh demand.
searchBrief: Search existing powered shells or enterprise facilities near validated HPC customers, especially in current operating/partner markets; treat land-only proposals as low priority until acquisition role is confirmed.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Assumption that high-density services imply appetite for a standalone land option.
Inference: No customer demand within practical network/operations geography.
Inference: Cooling retrofit cannot support current cabinet requirements economically.
buyerQuestions: Are you currently acquiring real estate, leasing partner capacity or both?
Which markets have contracted demand beyond existing inventory?
What are today’s density, liquid-cooling and electrical distribution requirements?

name: Netrality Data Centers
role: Core interconnection developer/operator and building acquirer
strategy: Acquires strategic urban interconnection buildings and expands their capacity. Network ecosystem and latency-sensitive customers are the central investment thesis; low-cost power alone is a poor match.
scale: Current company page reports 18 properties, 3.3 million square feet and over 100 MW portfolio capacity. July 2025 Indianapolis expansion: 1 MW critical capacity, 3,800 sq ft, up to 30 kW/cabinet. Portfolio total is not a site requirement.

publishedRequirements.fact: Netrality explicitly describes acquisition of strategically located core network-interconnection facilities for latency-sensitive businesses.
The Indy Telcom Center expansion adds 1 MW critical capacity and uses localized cooling to support up to 30 kW/cabinet.

inferredPreferences: An operating carrier hotel or adjacent urban expansion opportunity has value a remote greenfield site cannot easily replicate.
Existing tenants, cross-connects, carrier entrances and access rights are acquisition diligence priorities.
More MW may be less valuable than a small capacity increment at a congested interconnection point.
differentiators: Clear published acquisition type: core network-interconnection buildings.
Low-MW expansion within a network-dense existing campus.
Powered shell, colocation and wholesale products can coexist within the same building.
dealStructure: Direct property acquisitions and expansion; a pure land option is credible mainly when adjacent to an existing strategic hub or backed by a validated network relocation.
acquisitionSignal: Current acquisition strategy is explicit; Indianapolis expansion demonstrates investment within owned inventory, not an open rural site search.
searchBrief: Search urban carrier buildings, fiber meet-me-room assets and directly connected expansion tracts; document carriers, cross-connect economics, structural capacity and permitted generator/cooling yards.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: No established network ecosystem or economically constructible connection to one.
Inference: Site cannot support low-latency users despite ample power.
Inference: Physical expansion breaks tenant resiliency or requires prohibitively expensive migration.
buyerQuestions: Which interconnection nodes lack incremental power/space?
Would adjacent land be acquired, or only operating connected buildings?
Which carrier, tenant and cross-connect rights must transfer with the asset?

name: EdgeConneX
parentGroup: EQT-backed platform; project relationships include TA Digital Group and AdaniConneX
role: Customer-led developer/operator from edge to hyperscale
strategy: Builds capacity around customer geography, density and timing, with both metro-edge campuses and very large hyperscale projects. A site must fit a defined customer need rather than a universal EdgeConneX land template.
scale: Atlanta legacy campuses show mid-single-digit to tens-of-MW expansions; TA partnership announced 324 MW hyperscale campus. These are separate product scales; headline MW basis not consistently specified.

publishedRequirements.fact: EdgeConneX’s Atlanta materials describe metro proximity, regional fiber/cloud access, carrier-neutral service and rack-density capability.
TA Digital Group lists a July 2024 joint 324 MW Atlanta development announcement, demonstrating a partner-led land/power/entitlement model.

inferredPreferences: An edge deployment depends on end-user/network proximity; a hyperscale build depends on a named capacity block and customer contract. Do not combine their selection weights.
A developed land/power position can be useful to EdgeConneX through a specialist partner, but a raw option needs enough evidence to beat its established origination network.
The TA relationship means those two buyers may represent the same project exit; do not count them as statistically independent bids.
differentiators: Distinct edge and hyperscale product lanes.
Verified willingness to work with specialized land/power/entitlement partners.
Customer requirements, not a broad nationwide acreage threshold, define an actionable site.
dealStructure: Build-to-suit development, direct investment and project partnerships; no public blanket option-assignment policy.
acquisitionSignal: Atlanta joint development provides execution precedent; current open sites / geographies must be confirmed. Already announced campuses are competing supply.
searchBrief: Search only against a stated edge or hyperscale customer brief. For metros, prove latency/carriers; for campuses, provide transferable rights, phasing, entitlements and costed power delivery.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: Project presented to wrong product lane.
Inference: No customer-led reason to enter the geography.
Inference: Land/control package duplicates capacity already under development.
buyerQuestions: Is this requirement for metropolitan edge, AI inference or large-scale training?
Which required service date and customer ramp drive site choice?
Would EdgeConneX acquire the position directly or through a power / real-estate partner?
